# Project plan

## Start-up phase
<!--
Covering the planning phase, this section should provide a relatively
detailed plan of how work will start on the project. This section is
important because projects need to get up and running quickly.


 - [ ] Setting up collaboration platform inc. code for contributors etc.
 - [ ] License decisions
 - [ ] Reporting framework
-->
dabestr already exists as a full package and Github repository, so the project can be started straight away. A defining advantage is that the correct behaviour already exists. The current package is a rich regression specification: for every supported design and estimand we can freeze current point estimates, bootstrap distributions, confidence intervals, permutation results, and graphical semantics, and require the modernized code to reproduce them. This removes most of the scientific risk and makes each milestone objectively checkable. 


## Technical delivery
<!--
Covering the actual delivery of the project this section should
provide at least a high-level description of the implementation.

Including target dates is really important as you need to be committed
and the ISC need to have a means of tracking delivery
-->

Milestone 1 — Write the plan (Month 1–2). Write a public design document (published to the package website and opened as an RFC issue) specifying what a result contains, how to get information out of it, and how plots will use it. Acceptance: design document published; community comment period opened; committee-visible.

Milestone 2 — Reference regression corpus (Month 2–3). Deliverable: Record today’s outputs (estimates, intervals, figures) for every supported analysis as automatic tests (the “regression corpus”). Acceptance: corpus reproducible from a tagged commit.

Milestone 3 — Build the new standardized result object (Month 3–5). Create the new result object, separate from plotting, with simple functions that return effect sizes, intervals, and resampled data as tidy tables. Acceptance: all Milestone-2 regression checks pass; documented accessors covered by tests.

Milestone 4 — Visualization refactored onto the public standardized result object (Month 5–7). Rebuild the plots so they use only the new result object. Acceptance: rendered figures match the frozen graphical corpus; no plotting code reads undocumented internals.

Milestone 5 — Backward-compatibility and deprecation path (Month 6–8). Keep existing scripts running, with clear warnings before anything is retired. Simplify the delta–delta input. Acceptance: existing user scripts and the current tutorials run unmodified; migration guide published.

Milestone 6 — Documentation, maintenance infrastructure, and CRAN release (Month 8–9). Improve the docs, add a changelog and contributor guide, fix SD vs SEM/BSE wording in tutorials, and release on CRAN. Acceptance: package on CRAN; docs and changelog live; contributor guide published.


## Other aspects

<!--
How will you ensure that your work is available to the widest number
of people? Please specify the open-source or creative commons license(s)
you will use, how you will host your code so that others can contribute,
and how you will publicize your work. We encourage you to plan content
to be shared quarterly on the R Consortium blog.

 - [ ] Announcement post
 - [ ] Delivery blog post
 - [ ] Social media
 - [ ] UseR!
 - [ ] ISC meetings
-->
Everything is developed in the open under Apache-2.0, with issues and pull requests welcome; design documents and the migration guide are published on the package website. We will post an announcement and a delivery post on the R Consortium blog, share quarterly progress, announce through the package’s existing user channels and social media, propagate improvements to estimationstats.com (which is built on dabestr), and present at useR! or a similar venue and at ISC meetings (travel funded outside this grant). Beyond funding, the ISC could help by circulating the Milestone 1 design to reviewers with interests in tidy design, S7, and statistical-software architecture, and by advising on emerging community conventions for result objects.

## Budget & funding plan

<!--
Note that the maximum grant is $10k USD. The proposal should be in USD.

Outline the milestones for development and how much funding will be
required for each stage (as payments will be tied to project milestone
completion). This also helps the ISC in the event of partial funding. 
Each milestone should specify the work to be done and the
expected outcomes, providing enough detail for the ISC to understand
the scope of the project work and assess the likelihood of success.

We expect that most of the budget will be allocated
for labor costs. We do not cover indirect costs. The ISC grants cannot
cover such things as travel, lodging, food, journal publication fees,
or personal hardware. Cloud services may be covered if they are specific
to the project and the project period. The ISC reserves the right to vet
how funds are used for each project separately. If in doubt, please reach
out to us.
-->

We request USD $10,000 for developer labor only, with no hardware, cloud, travel, publication, or indirect costs. The project needs roughly 0.4 FTE over nine months from an existing maintainer; the grant funds part of this and the ACCLAB team contributes the remainder.

Funds follow the ISC’s standard schedule: 50% ($5,000) on signing and 50% ($5,000) on completion. The per-milestone allocation lets the ISC fund the project in part if needed (e.g. Milestones 1–3, the minimum viable product).
